newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish yields may rise despite minfin - c.bank deal.
newsitem.headline: Polish yields may rise despite minfin - c.bank deal.

text.p: Polish T-bill yields, which rose a point over the last month, may still have some room to grow even after the treasury moved to plug a gap in commercial demand for its paper by selling bills to the central bank, dealers said.

Earlier on Thursday a source, who asked not to be named, said the ministry offered to sell T-bills to the National Bank of Poland, but said the transaction would likely not be as large as the two billion zloty sale done at the end of 1996.
The finance ministry would not confirm or deny that it had offered to sell the paper and the NBP was not immidiately available for comment.
Analysts said that the benchmark 52-week T-bill yields would likely top out around 21.30 percent, up from an average of 20.92 at this Monday's primary tender.

"It seems the finance ministry needs money fast...(but) yield growth is not likely to stop. It could slow, with the region of 21.30 percent definately achievable," said Piotr Korcz, fixed income dealer at Bank Handlowy.
Several dealers said foreign investors would purchase large amounts of the benchmark only if yields rose to 21.5 percent.
"The pace of yield growth is likely to slow, but yields will still increase, especially because the ministry increased its T-bill offer in March," said Wojciech Labryga, dealer at Bank Slaski SA.
Under Polish law the central bank has to accept any finance ministry bill offers up to two percent of expenditures in the 1997 national budget, roughly 2.5 bilion zlotys.

Investor demand has remained low at recent primary auctions despite yield increases as banks filled portfolios with more attractive central bank NBP-bills, whose yields remained at a flat yield curve of 22.00 percent for 3- to 9-month paper.
The ministry had earlier said that it aimed to finance the budget deficit through the NBP only as a last resort and that it would not use debt instruments which mature past 1997.
The finance ministry sold 2.3 billion zlotys, in nominal terms, worth of its bills since the start of February against an offer of 5.2 billion zlotys.

Dealers said that any transaction between the finance ministry and the NBP would not likely cause the central bank to tighten its monetary policy further after it raised obligatory reserves for commercial banks on February 28.

"Right now nobody expects the central bank to increase official interest rates or reserves requrements at least until it can evaluate figures for the first quarter of 1997," said Radoslaw Radziszewski, deputy chief-dealer at Pekao SA.

December's sale of T-bills to the central bank skewed the bank's money supply estimates off course and caused it to raise obligatory reserves on zloty call deposits by three points to 20 percent and on double currency deposits to four percent.
